chunks: With the preceding chain of narration, from Ali ibn Mahzyar, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Yunus ibn Ya’qub, from Shu’ayb al-Aqarqufi, he said: I said to Abu Abdillah Ja’far ibn Muhammad, peace be upon them both:
I heard someone narrate from Abu Dharr that he used to say: People hate three things, while I love them: I love death, and I love poverty, and I love ordeals.

So he, peace be upon him, said: Indeed, this is not according to what people think. Rather, what he meant by his saying ’I love death’ is that death in obedience to Allah is more beloved to me than life in disobedience to Allah, and ordeal in obedience to Allah is more beloved to me than health in disobedience to Allah, and poverty in obedience to Allah is more beloved to me than wealth in disobedience to Allah.

key_terms.بَلَاء: ordeal/trial - hardship or test from Allah
key_terms.طَاعَة: obedience (to Allah) - willing compliance with divine commands
key_terms.مَوْت: death - the end of worldly life

ai.seo_question: What did Abu Dharr really mean when he said he loves death, poverty, and ordeals?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (a.s.) clarifies Abu Dharr’s famous paradoxical saying about loving death, poverty, and ordeals. Speaking to Shu’ayb al-Aqarqufi, the Imam explains that Abu Dharr’s words are widely misunderstood by those who take them literally. The Imam reveals that Abu Dharr’s true meaning was conditional: he preferred death, hardship, and poverty that come in the path of obedience to Allah over life, health, and wealth that accompany disobedience. This reframing transforms a seemingly ascetic or masochistic statement into a profound expression of spiritual priorities, showing that the value of any worldly condition depends entirely on whether it leads one closer to or further from God.
